docs.title: manifolds-rs
docs.text:
Dimensionality reduction for single-cell and computational biology. The Rust crate does the work. This is a scikit-learn shaped layer over it.

Eleven algorithms on the CPU, five of them with GPU variants where the neighbour search and the Adam update move to the device. No CUDA runtime to install: the GPU backend is wgpu, so it runs on Metal, Vulkan or DX12 and ships in the ordinary wheel.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv pip install manifolds-rs

Wheels are built for Linux and macOS, x86_64 and arm64 on both, against Python 3.10 and up. numpy and beartype are the only runtime dependencies.

docs.title: Thirty seconds
docs.text:
import manifolds_rs as mf

X, labels = mf.datasets.clustered(20_000, dim=50, n_clusters=12)

embedding = mf.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1).fit_transform(X)

Parameters in the constructor, data in fit, an (n_samples, n_components) array back. get_params and set_params are there, so clone and Pipeline work without scikit-learn being an install requirement.

docs.title: The parameter story
docs.text:
The knobs people actually turn are ordinary constructor arguments. Everything else lives in frozen dataclasses, one per group, and anything you leave alone keeps the crate's default:

mf.UMAP(
    n_neighbors=30,
    ann="hnsw",
    nn_params=mf.NeighbourParams(m=32, ef_search=200),
    optim_params=mf.UmapOptim(gamma=1.5, neg_sample_rate=10),
)

Every parameter has exactly one home. If it is a constructor argument it is not in the group, so there is never a question of which wins.

docs.title: AnnData / scanpy
docs.text:
mf.umap and mf.tsne are drop-ins for sc.tl.umap and sc.tl.tsne. They write the same slots, so everything downstream (sc.pl.umap, sc.pl.tsne, sc.pl.embedding) works unchanged. They need the anndata extra; scanpy itself is not a dependency.

uv pip install 'manifolds-rs[anndata]'

docs.title: UMAP
docs.text:
import scanpy as sc
import manifolds_rs as mf

sc.pp.pca(adata)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=15)
mf.umap(adata)
sc.pl.umap(adata, color="leiden")

Like scanpy's, mf.umap embeds the sc.pp.neighbors graph rather than searching again. It reads the neighbour indices and distances back out of obsp["distances"] and the crate builds its own fuzzy graph from them, so n_neighbors and the metric are whatever sc.pp.neighbors used. Scanpy counts the cell itself and this does not, so n_neighbors=15 there is recorded as 14 here. The representation (use_rep, n_pcs) comes from the same uns["neighbors"]["params"] and feeds the initialisation.

obsp["distances"] has to hold the same number of neighbours on every row, which it does for sc.pp.neighbors with its default settings. A ragged graph is an error.

docs.title: t-SNE
docs.text:
mf.tsne(adata)  # obsm["X_pca"]
mf.tsne(adata, n_pcs=30)  # the first 30 PCs
mf.tsne(adata, use_rep="X_scVI")  # any dense obsm key, or "X"

mf.tsne does its own 3 * perplexity neighbour search on the representation, as sc.tl.tsne does. The 15-neighbour graph from sc.pp.neighbors is far too narrow for t-SNE at the usual perplexity. There is no automatic PCA: without obsm["X_pca"] and no use_rep, it raises and tells you to run sc.pp.pca.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
mf.umap(adata, device="gpu")
mf.tsne(adata, device="gpu", approx="fft_3k_gpu")

device="gpu" swaps in UMAPGpu / TSNEGpu. See GPU acceleration for what runs on the device and in which precision.

docs.title: What gets written
docs.text:
Call obsm uns mf.umap(adata) "X_umap" "umap" mf.tsne(adata) "X_tsne" "tsne" key_added="foo" "foo" "foo"

uns[...]["params"] holds the estimator's scalar parameters, plus device and neighbors_key (UMAP) or use_rep / n_pcs (t-SNE). Only scalars are kept, so the result survives write_h5ad. UMAP's a and b are not stored: the crate fits them from min_dist and spread and does not hand them back.

copy=True returns a modified copy and leaves adata alone.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Other constructor arguments of the estimator go through as keywords:

mf.umap(adata, n_epochs=200, init="pca", optim_params=mf.UmapOptim(gamma=1.5))
mf.tsne(adata, learning_rate=500.0)

Unknown names raise, same as the estimator constructors. The neighbour graph comes from adata, which sets two limits: n_neighbors is taken from the graph and raises TypeError if you pass it, and ann and metric are accepted but do nothing, since the search never runs.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
25,000 cells from mf.datasets.clustered(25_000, dim=50, n_clusters=8), sc.pp.pca(n_comps=30) and sc.pp.neighbors(n_neighbors=15) beforehand, not timed. Three repeats per row at seeds 0, 1 and 2, after an untimed warm-up (numba JIT for umap-learn, wgpu device initialisation). Cluster separation is the mean between-centroid distance over the mean within-cluster spread; higher means the clusters sit further apart than they are wide.

Call Time (s) Cluster separation sc.tl.umap 10.64 ± 0.02 19.83 ± 0.90 mf.umap 1.48 ± 0.07 26.04 ± 0.27 mf.umap(device="gpu") 0.43 ± 0.01 19.06 ± 0.29 sc.tl.tsne(n_jobs=10) 47.21 ± 1.07 11.14 ± 0.00 mf.tsne 9.73 ± 0.27 8.71 ± 0.23 mf.tsne(device="gpu") 12.18 ± 0.32 8.72 ± 0.24 mf.tsne(device="gpu", approx="fft_3k_gpu") 4.89 ± 0.06 8.34 ± 0.14

Mean ± sd over the three repeats. Run on an Apple M1 Max (10 cores), scanpy 1.11.5. Defaults on both sides, with two things worth knowing: scanpy runs UMAP for 200 epochs above 10,000 cells where mf.umap runs 500 with its default Adam optimiser (the SGD optimisers drop to 200 there too), and sc.tl.tsne was given n_jobs=10 since its default is single-threaded. One synthetic dataset on one machine; measure on your own data before relying on it.

docs.title: Choosing an algorithm
docs.text: Ten of them, and the honest summary is that three cover most work. Here is how to pick without running all ten.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: Your data Start with Cell types you expect to separate UMAP A differentiation trajectory, or anything continuous PHATE You care about the arrangement of clusters, not just the clusters PaCMAP As PaCMAP, but neighbouring clusters keep bleeding into each other LocalMAP You want the tightest possible local structure and nothing else TSNE Relative density in the plot should mean something DensMAP t-SNE clusters, but in a sensible arrangement DREAMS You want the spectral embedding itself, not a layout of it DiffusionMaps You want a force-directed graph layout, scanpy draw_graph style ForceAtlas2 t-SNE-like clusters on a lot of points, fast NCVis

docs.title: What each one is actually doing
docs.text:
UMAP builds a fuzzy simplicial set from the kNN graph and optimises a cross-entropy against it. The spectral initialisation is where most of its global structure comes from, and it is the default here for that reason. Fast, well understood, and the sensible first thing to run.

densMAP is UMAP plus a term correlating the embedding's local radii with the original space's. Plain UMAP is free to stretch a sparse region and squash a dense one, so relative density in a UMAP plot means nothing at all. If you are about to say "this cluster is tighter, so those cells are more homogeneous", you want densMAP. The term only switches on for the last 30% of the run, so it corrects a settled embedding rather than fighting the layout.

t-SNE optimises a KL divergence between neighbourhood distributions. It is the best of these at local structure and the worst at global: distances between t-SNE clusters carry very little information, and cluster sizes carry none. The learning rate here defaults to max(N / 12, 200) rather than a fixed 200, so it does not need retuning as the dataset grows. Two-dimensional only.

den-SNE is the same density correction applied to t-SNE. The default weight is much smaller than densMAP's because its gradient has neither a log epsilon nor gradient clipping to absorb a collapsed radius, not because the effect is meant to be weaker.

DREAMS is t-SNE with a pull towards a global reference embedding, PCA unless you hand one in. You keep the clusters and get a sensible arrangement of them. lambda_ slides from plain t-SNE at 0 to the reference at 1.

PHATE powers a diffusion operator to time t, takes the potential distance between the resulting distributions, and lays those out with MDS. That is a completely different object from a kNN graph layout, and it is why trajectories and branch points survive PHATE that t-SNE tears into blobs. If your biology is continuous, this is the one.

PaCMAP uses three kinds of pair: near pairs pull, further pairs push, and mid-near pairs hold the global arrangement together. Their weight starts high and decays across the first phase, which is what lets it keep global structure without leaning on a spectral initialisation. PCA init is close to required; random init throws away most of the advantage.

LocalMAP is PaCMAP with a different last phase. Further pairs that already sit more than max_distance apart in the embedding get resampled, and the near-pair forces are scaled by their embedding distance. The upshot: clusters that PaCMAP leaves touching get pulled apart, and the global arrangement from the first two phases stays. Same arguments as PaCMAP plus max_distance.

Diffusion maps is the spectral embedding PHATE builds on. Reach for it when you want the diffusion coordinates themselves rather than a 2-D picture of them. The knob worth understanding is alpha: 0 gives the normalised graph Laplacian, 0.5 the Fokker-Planck operator, 1 the Laplace-Beltrami operator, which is the one that removes the influence of sampling density.

ForceAtlas2 is Gephi's force-directed layout, run on the same fuzzy kNN graph UMAP builds, which is what scanpy's draw_graph does. Every pair of points repels, edges attract, and gravity keeps disconnected components from drifting off. Unlike UMAP there is no edge sampling: every edge is visited every epoch. lin_log=True pulls communities tighter; scaling_ratio spreads the whole layout. graph_params.mix_weight has to stay at 1, because the layout needs a symmetric graph. Two-dimensional only.

NCVis is noise-contrastive estimation on the plain kNN graph, made undirected and unweighted. Each edge pulls its two points together and draws uniform negatives that push apart, with a normalisation constant learned on the side. The defaults are NCVis+'s, and the one that matters is the PCA start, scaled as a whole so the components keep their ratios: that is where the global arrangement comes from, and init="random" throws much of it away. n_negative is the time against local quality knob. The optimiser is hogwild, so a fixed seed reproduces only with set_num_threads(1).

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Rough ordering on the same data, dominated by different things:

  • TSNE, DensNE and ForceAtlas2 pay for the Barnes-Hut tree every epoch. For the first two, approx="qd" caps the tree depth and computes repulsion once per leaf instead of once per point; on 20k points that halved the optimiser time. approx="fft" and "fft_3k" swap the tree for an FFT on an interpolation grid, linear in the number of points.
  • UMAP, DensMAP, PaCMAP and LocalMAP pay for the neighbour search and then a cheap per-edge update. The parallel Adam optimiser is the default. optimiser="sgd_parallel" runs the reference SGD lock-free over all threads, at the price of a different embedding on every run.
  • NCVis pays for the neighbour search, the PCA start and 50 epochs of hogwild SGD. Every edge draws n_negative negatives on average, so that is the knob that sets the layout time.
  • PHATE pays for the powering, the potential distances and the MDS, which is why it runs on 2048 landmarks by default. n_landmarks=None runs the full operator, whose dense distance matrix grows with the square of the sample count.
  • DiffusionMaps pays for an eigendecomposition of the sparse operator, and runs on the full operator unless you set n_landmarks.

For all of them, past a few hundred thousand points the neighbour search dominates. The defaults ("nndescent", "ivf" for the t-SNE family, PaCMAP, LocalMAP and PHATE) are built for that; "hnsw" is the alternative, and "rinnd" is worth a try on x86. Or build the graph once with knn_graph and hand it to each estimator.

docs.title: What none of them do
docs.text: Project new points. There is no transform. Embedding new data means refitting on the combined set, which moves the existing coordinates too, and any method that appears to avoid that is doing something to the new points that is not the operation the old ones went through.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text: The details that will otherwise bite you.

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
float32 in, float32 out. float64 in, float64 out. Anything else, integers included, is promoted to float64 rather than narrowed.

The design matrix picks the precision for the pipeline at any size, including the optimiser. There is no separate knob for it.

Worth knowing on large data: float32 kept up. On real single cell PCA at 1M cells, UMAP, t-SNE, PaCMAP and ForceAtlas2 scored the same in both precisions, while float64 took up to 51% longer and 46% more memory. That is one dataset, and nothing above 1M was tested.

Four exceptions:

  • The neighbour search runs in float32 on every backend bar "exhaustive", and the distances are cast back up. So knn_graph on float64 input returns float64 with float32 precision in the values. Want float64 ground truth? Use "exhaustive".
  • PCA initialisation and the randomised SVDs always run in float64, then cast the result back. The float32 factorisations break down at about 520k samples.
  • The GPU estimators cast to float32 at any size. That is the only silent narrowing of your input in the package.
  • approx="fft_3k_mlx" optimises in float32 on the device, whatever you pass.

docs.title: Distances
docs.text:
knn_graph returns true distances in whatever metric you asked for. The Euclidean backends compute squared distances internally, because that does not change the ordering they sort on, and the square root is taken before the distances reach you.

So a graph you build yourself and hand to fit should hold true distances too.

Metrics available: "euclidean"/"l2", "cosine" and "manhattan"/"l1". Manhattan needs "nndescent", "rinnd", "hnsw" or "exhaustive" as the backend. PHATE, PHATEGpu and DiffusionMaps with landmarks raise ValueError on it.

docs.title: Reusing the neighbour graph
docs.text:
Past a few hundred thousand points the neighbour search is most of the runtime. Build it once:

ind, dist = mf.knn_graph(X, k=60, ann="hnsw")

umap = mf.UMAP(n_neighbors=15).fit_transform(X, knn_indices=ind, knn_distances=dist)
pacmap = mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform(X, knn_indices=ind, knn_distances=dist)

Three things to get right. Build the graph as wide as the widest consumer needs: 3 * perplexity for the t-SNE family, n_near + 50 for PaCMAP and 6k + 5 for PHATE, since its kernel keeps anything just past the k-th neighbour.

UMAP, DensMAP, ForceAtlas2 and NCVis cut a wider graph to n_neighbors, keeping the nearest, and print a warning to stderr saying so. A graph you build yourself has to be sorted by distance for that to mean anything.

And the graph must be complete: a row an approximate backend could not fill is padded with -1, and that is refused rather than quietly dropped, because a hole in the graph is not something these algorithms can embed.

Handing in the graph an estimator would have built itself produces a bit-identical embedding. It is a shortcut, not a different algorithm.

docs.title: Choosing a neighbour backend
docs.text:
The default follows k. Estimators that ask for a small neighbourhood (UMAP, densMAP, diffusion maps, ForceAtlas2, NCVis) default to "nndescent". t-SNE, den-SNE and DREAMS ask for 3 * perplexity neighbours, PaCMAP and LocalMAP for n_near + 50 and PHATE for 6k + 5, and those default to "ivf", which holds up better at that size.

"kmknn" is exact and holds up well into the hundreds of thousands, which surprises people who assume exact means slow. "exhaustive" is for ground truth. "hnsw", "annoy" and "balltree" are there for the cases where they win.

Default wheels also carry "rinnd", the NN-Descent from rinnd. Its SIMD kernels target x86 (AVX2), so on x86 it is worth trying in place of "nndescent". rinnd_available() says whether your build has it. Both NN-Descents take nnd_n_trees, the number of trees seeding the graph; left at None, "nndescent" follows the umap-learn / scanpy rule and "rinnd" its own, which plants fewer.

Each has its own knobs in NeighbourParams, and only the ones belonging to your chosen backend do anything. Setting ef_search while running "annoy" is harmless and has no effect.

docs.title: Parameter groups
docs.text:
Every parameter has exactly one home. If it is a constructor argument on the estimator it is not in the group, and vice versa. So:

  • metric is on the estimator, not NeighbourParams.dist_metric.
  • n_epochs and learning_rate are on the estimator, not UmapOptim.
  • min_dist is on the estimator, not UmapOptim. It and spread feed the curve fit that produces a and b; letting you move min_dist without refitting them would be the one combination that is always wrong. Pinning a and b directly is still available in UmapOptim for anyone who means it.

A field left at None in a group is not sent at all and the crate's default applies. A misspelled field is a TypeError naming the field.

docs.title: Nulls that mean something
docs.text:
Three parameters take None as a real value rather than "use the default":

  • PHATE(decay=None) selects a binary connectivity kernel instead of the alpha-decay one.
  • PHATE(n_landmarks=None) runs the full operator instead of landmarks.
  • PaCMAP(range_=None) hands the range to the initialisation's own default.

Everywhere else None means "let the crate decide".

docs.title: Verbosity
docs.text:
verbose=0 is quiet. verbose=1 prints each stage with its timing, plus the optimiser's epochs every 50. verbose=2 adds the parameters, the neighbour index internals and the landmark selection. Anything else raises ValueError. Warnings print at every level, to stderr.

verbose=1 or 2 writes progress to the process stdout, not sys.stdout. In Jupyter that lands in the terminal running the kernel, not in the notebook. This is the core printing directly and there is nothing this layer can do about it short of capturing a file descriptor.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
The core is rayon throughout. By default it uses rayon's global pool, sized from RAYON_NUM_THREADS or the core count.

mf.set_num_threads(4)  # cap it, for a shared machine or a job scheduler
mf.num_threads()
mf.set_num_threads(0)  # back to the global pool

The GIL is released for the entire computation, so an embedding running in a background thread does not block the interpreter.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
On the CPU, same seed, same data, same parameters gives a bit-identical embedding. The seed fixes the initialisation, the negative sampling and anything randomised in the neighbour build.

On the GPU, the coordinates can differ between runs at the same seed. The structure does not.

The source is the neighbour search, not the optimiser: the GPU Adam update is bit-stable given a fixed graph, and the device searches are not always stable at scale. Two runs agree on about 99.4% of neighbour slots; where they disagree, the two candidates sit a median 0.4% apart in distance, and recall against exhaustive ground truth matches to the fourth decimal.

What that means in practice, measured on 20k points in 50 dimensions across 12 clusters, two runs at the same seed:

  • k-means on either embedding recovers the same partition. Adjusted Rand index between the two clusterings: 1.0000.
  • Cluster separation matches: silhouette 0.849 versus 0.858.
  • Individual points can swap places within a dense cluster, so point-for-point neighbour lists are not identical.

On a swiss roll, both runs came back bit-identical and preserved the manifold equally (0.623 versus 0.628). So it is data-dependent rather than guaranteed either way.

If you need the coordinates themselves to be reproducible, use the CPU estimators, or build the graph once with knn_graph and hand it in. Do not turn a plot into a figure and expect the pixels back; do rely on the clusters, the branches and the separations being there.

Across dtypes reproducibility does not hold either way: float32 and float64 runs of the same configuration will differ, as they should.

Across releases it does not hold either: 0.5.0 changed the eigensolver behind the spectral initialisation, PHATE and diffusion maps, so coordinates differ from 0.4.x at the same seed. 0.6.0 moved PCA initialisation and the randomised SVDs to float64, so float32 runs differ from 0.5.0. It also moved the neighbour search to float32, so float64 runs differ too. 0.6.1 fixed the automatic t of PHATE and DiffusionMaps from 5000 points up, and moved it to float64, so those runs differ from 0.6.0 unless t is pinned. 0.7.0 changed the fuzzy graph bandwidth, the IVF and NN-Descent graphs and the k-means behind the spectral landmarks, so every estimator differs from 0.6.x at the same seed.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• ValueError for most things you can fix by changing an argument, including everything the neighbour search rejects.
  • ConvergenceError when a spectral decomposition ran but did not get there, which usually means degenerate data: duplicate points, or a disconnected landmark set. It subclasses ManifoldsRsError, which is also what the rest of the core's errors come as, for example DensNE(approx="fft_3k_mlx").
  • TypeError for a bad parameter name or type.
  • NotFittedError for reading embedding_ before fit. It subclasses both ValueError and AttributeError, matching scikit-learn's.

docs.title: What is not in the wheel
docs.text:
The MLX backends. They link mlx-c dynamically, so they only come with a source build on Apple Silicon; see GPU acceleration.

Parametric UMAP exists in the crate but is not yet bound.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Everything below runs against the built-in generators, so you can paste it without finding a dataset first.

docs.title: Your first embedding
docs.text:
import manifolds_rs as mf

X, labels = mf.datasets.clustered(20_000, dim=50, n_clusters=12, seed=0)

embedding = mf.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1).fit_transform(X)
embedding.shape  # (20000, 2)

fit_transform is the method you want. fit plus embedding_ says the same thing in scikit-learn's shape if that suits the surrounding code better.

docs.title: Scoring it, rather than squinting at it
docs.text:
A picture of an embedding is not evidence. These generators hand back ground truth, so use it.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors


def preservation(X, embedding, k=15):
    """Fraction of each point's high-dimensional neighbours still nearby."""
    hi = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(X).kneighbors(return_distance=False)
    lo = (
        NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(embedding).kneighbors(return_distance=False)
    )
    return np.mean([len(set(a) & set(b)) for a, b in zip(hi, lo)]) / k

Run that over the swiss roll, which is a genuine manifold, and it separates the algorithms cleanly. 5000 points, defaults throughout, mean over four dataset seeds:

neighbourhood preservation TSNE 0.83 PaCMAP 0.76 NCVis 0.72 UMAP 0.68 ForceAtlas2 0.58 PHATE 0.53

t-SNE wins on local structure because that is the only thing it optimises. PHATE comes last for the opposite reason: it is built for the smooth global picture, not for keeping each point's 15 nearest neighbours.

Now run the same metric over 12 Gaussian clusters in 50D and it collapses for everyone: 0.02 for UMAP, 0.13 for t-SNE, 0.02 for PaCMAP. Meanwhile silhouette against the known labels is 0.91, 0.81 and 0.95.

That is not three algorithms failing. Inside an isotropic Gaussian blob in 50 dimensions there is no local ordering to preserve: which 15 of your thousand-odd cluster-mates happen to be nearest is close to arbitrary, so no embedding can keep it. The clusters come apart perfectly regardless.

The lesson is to pick the metric that matches what you are claiming. Quote neighbourhood preservation on manifold data and cluster separation on cluster data, and be suspicious of any benchmark that reports one number.

docs.title: Comparing algorithms on the same graph
docs.text:
The neighbour search is most of the runtime on anything large, and every estimator accepts a precomputed graph. Build it once:

ind, dist = mf.knn_graph(X, k=90, ann="hnsw")

results = {}
for name, estimator in [
    ("umap", mf.UMAP(n_neighbors=15)),
    ("pacmap", mf.PaCMAP()),
    ("tsne", mf.TSNE()),
]:
    results[name] = estimator.fit_transform(X, knn_indices=ind, knn_distances=dist)

Build the graph as wide as the widest estimator needs. UMAP cuts it to n_neighbors and warns that it did. See the guide.

docs.title: Trajectories
docs.text:
This is where the choice of algorithm stops being cosmetic.

X, branch = mf.datasets.trajectory(10_000, topology="bifurcation", dim=50)

phate = mf.PHATE(k=5).fit_transform(X)
tsne = mf.TSNE(perplexity=30).fit_transform(X)

PHATE keeps the branch points connected. t-SNE will give you a set of blobs that happen to correspond to positions along the trajectory, with the connectivity gone. Neither is wrong; they are answering different questions.

docs.title: Density that means something
docs.text:
X, t = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(10_000, density_bias=2.5)

plain = mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X)
dens = mf.DensMAP(lambda_=2.0).fit_transform(X)

The roll is deliberately sampled unevenly. In the plain UMAP the dense end and the sparse end come out looking similar, because UMAP is free to rescale locally. In the densMAP they do not.

docs.title: Turning the obscure knobs
docs.text:
mf.UMAP(
    n_neighbors=30,
    ann="hnsw",
    nn_params=mf.NeighbourParams(m=32, ef_construction=400, ef_search=200),
    graph_params=mf.UmapGraph(local_connectivity=2.0),
    optim_params=mf.UmapOptim(gamma=1.5, neg_sample_rate=10),
)

Anything you leave out of a group keeps the crate's default, and a group you do not pass at all is the same as passing an empty one. A misspelled field is a TypeError naming the field, not a silent no-op.

docs.title: Capping threads
docs.text:
mf.set_num_threads(4)  # for a shared machine or a job scheduler
mf.num_threads()  # 4
mf.set_num_threads(0)  # back to rayon's global pool

docs.title: AnnData functions
docs.text: Need the anndata extra. See AnnData / scanpy.

docs.title: umap
docs.text:
umap(
    adata: AnnData,
    *,
    n_components: int = 2,
    min_dist: int | float = 0.5,
    spread: int | float = 1.0,
    neighbors_key: str = "neighbors",
    key_added: str | None = None,
    device: str = "cpu",
    seed: int = 42,
    verbose: int = 0,
    copy: bool = False,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> AnnData | None

UMAP on the sc.pp.neighbors graph, stored the way sc.tl.umap does.

The neighbour graph is taken from obsp rather than searched again, so n_neighbors and the metric are whatever sc.pp.neighbors used. The representation (use_rep / n_pcs) is read from the same uns[neighbors_key]["params"]; it feeds the initialisation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default adata AnnData

Annotated data matrix, after sc.pp.neighbors.

required n_components int

Output dimensionality.

2 min_dist int | float

How tightly points may pack. Fits the repulsion curve with spread.

0.5 spread int | float

Scale of the embedding relative to min_dist.

1.0 neighbors_key str

Where sc.pp.neighbors stored its results in uns.

'neighbors' key_added str | None

The default optimiser is the multi-threaded Adam one, which is where most of the speed comes from; "sgd" follows umap-learn's edge sampling schedule and is slower. Bases: BaseEmbedding

NCVis: noise-contrastive estimation on the kNN graph.

The graph is the plain kNN graph made undirected, with no edge weights. Each edge pulls its endpoints together and draws uniform negatives that push apart, weighted by how likely the pair is data rather than noise under the kernel 1 / (1 + a d^(2b)) and a normalisation constant learned along the way. The negatives ramp up with the cube of progress, so most of them land in the last epochs.

Defaults are NCVis+'s (Pedersen's fork of Artemenkov & Panov's NCVis): a PCA start scaled to std 10 on its first axis, min_dist 0.001, a learning rate of 2 and on average 10 negatives per edge. The PCA start is what keeps the global structure; init="random" loses much of it.

The optimiser is lock-free (hogwild) over all threads, so a fixed seed gives the same embedding only on one thread (set_num_threads(1)).

docs.title: GPU acceleration
GPU acceleration¶
docs.text: Five estimators run part of their work on the GPU: UMAPGpu, DensMAPGpu, TSNEGpu, DREAMSGpu and PHATEGpu. The backend is wgpu, so there is no CUDA runtime to install, and the same wheel runs on Metal, Vulkan and DX12. This vignette covers what actually moves to the device, what it buys you, and the sharp edges.

docs.title: What moves to the device¶
docs.text:
Not everything.

  • UMAPGpu and DensMAPGpu: the neighbour search and the optimiser. "adam_gpu" (default) is the parallel Adam on the device, "adam_v06_gpu" the umap-learn 0.6 Adam. The CPU names still work and run the optimiser on the CPU after a GPU search. Graph construction and initialisation stay on the CPU. densMAP's density term runs on the device with "adam_gpu"; the radii come back to the host in between so the correlation statistics can accumulate in float64. The 0.6 Adam has no density term, so DensMAPGpu refuses both "adam_v06" names.
  • TSNEGpu and DREAMSGpu: the neighbour search always. With approx="fft_3k_gpu" the whole optimisation stays on the device too: the three-kernel FFT repulsion, with the embedding resident between epochs. The other approx values run on the CPU after the GPU search.
  • PHATEGpu: the neighbour search and, with spectral landmarks, the randomised SVD and k-means of the landmark selection. Diffusion time, powering, MDS and interpolation stay on the CPU.

Same data on both sides first, to see the pictures agree.

docs.title: Is it faster?¶
docs.text: That depends on whether the neighbour search and the optimiser were your bottleneck. On a few thousand points they won't be, and the transfers make the GPU slower than the CPU. Here are 200k points in 50 dimensions, one run each, wall time in seconds, neighbour search included.

docs.title: Precision¶
docs.text: WGSL has no float64, so the GPU estimators run in float32 at any size. fit casts your input down, float64 included, and the embedding comes back as float32. That is the only silent narrowing of your input in the package. If it matters for your data, stay on the CPU estimators, which keep your dtype. PCA initialisation still runs in float64 on the CPU and is cast back.

docs.title: Reproducibility¶
docs.text: GPU embeddings are reproducible in structure, not always in coordinates. The device neighbour searches are not bit-stable at scale, and 500 epochs of Adam turn a tiny difference in the graph into visibly different coordinates. The clusters, branches and separations come back; the exact positions may not. The Adam update itself is bit-stable given a fixed graph, so hand in a pre-computed graph and a GPU run is reproducible too.

docs.title: Neighbour backends¶
docs.text: The device backends are not the CPU ones with a suffix. "nndescent_gpu" runs NN-Descent on the device and is the default for UMAPGpu, DensMAPGpu and PHATEGpu. TSNEGpu and DREAMSGpu ask for 3 * perplexity neighbours and default to "ivf_gpu", which holds up better at that k. "exhaustive_gpu" is the third. A CPU-only name like "hnsw" is an error, not a silent fallback. The knobs live in NeighbourParamsGpu, a different set from the CPU NeighbourParams.

docs.title: Mixing CPU and GPU¶
docs.text: The neighbour graph is two arrays, so build it wherever it is cheapest and hand it to whichever estimator you like. The graph above came from the CPU; here it feeds the GPU optimiser, and the GPU search is skipped entirely.

docs.title: Headless machines and CI¶
docs.text: gpu_available() returns False on a box with no adapter rather than raising, and the GPU estimators still import. That is deliberate: a hosted CI runner can prove the GPU wheel builds and degrades cleanly without a device. It cannot prove the kernels are correct. That needs a runner with a GPU.

docs.title: MLX on Apple Silicon¶
docs.text:
There is a second Apple GPU path, through MLX via mlx-c, and it is not in the published wheel. It links mlx-c dynamically, so a wheel carrying it fails to import on any Mac without the library. Build it yourself:

brew install mlx-c
maturin develop --release --features mlx

mf.mlx_available() is True only in an mlx build that found mlx-c. MLX is not a separate set of estimators; the CPU estimators gain a few extra names:

mf.UMAP(ann="nndescent_mlx", optimiser="adam_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.DensMAP(optimiser="adam_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.TSNE(ann="nndescent_mlx", approx="fft_3k_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.DREAMS(approx="fft_3k_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.PHATE(ann="nndescent_mlx", landmark_method="spectral_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.knn_graph(X, k=15, ann="ivf_mlx")

The neighbour backends are "exhaustive_mlx", "ivf_mlx" and "nndescent_mlx". TSNEGpu and DREAMSGpu take approx="fft_3k_mlx" as well, with the search on wgpu and the optimiser on MLX. PHATEGpu takes landmark_method="spectral_mlx" the same way. den-SNE has no MLX path, and DiffusionMaps keeps its landmark selection on the CPU. Everything MLX runs in float32. In a build without MLX these names are refused with a pointer to the build flag.

Is it worth the trouble? See the wgpu vs MLX benchmarks.

docs.title: Nearest neighbour searches¶
docs.text:
Python port of the R vignette Nearest neighbour searches in manifoldsR. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

kNN graphs sit underneath nearly every method in this package. UMAP, densMAP, t-SNE, PaCMAP, LocalMAP, PHATE, diffusion maps and ForceAtlas2 all start from one. This vignette walks through the backends, what each is good at, how exact the approximate ones are, and how to build a graph once and hand it to several estimators instead of recomputing it every time.

docs.title: Exhaustive search¶
docs.text: The simplest one. A flat index with SIMD distance kernels, so it is cache friendly and on small data it beats the approximate searches, which have to build an index first. knn_graph hands back indices and distances as two (n_samples, k) arrays, self excluded.

docs.title: Approximate searches¶
docs.text:
The package is built for large data and pulls its approximate searches from ann-search-rs. Five of them are exposed, on top of the two exact ones. Default wheels add a sixth, "rinnd", from Leland McInnes' rinnd:

Method Class Use case "balltree" Tree Small data, low dimensionality. "annoy" Tree A single-cell classic. Scales to a few hundred thousand points at low dimensionality. "hnsw" Graph Large data (500k and up), any dimensionality. Slower build, fast queries. The build uses a benign race. "nndescent" Graph The all-rounder from 100k points on. Default for UMAP, densMAP, ForceAtlas2 and diffusion maps. "rinnd" Graph rinnd's NN-Descent. Its SIMD kernels are tuned for x86 (AVX2), so it is the one to try there. mf.rinnd_available() says whether your build has it. "ivf" Cluster The index behind FAISS. Large data, any dimensionality. n_probes trades recall for speed. Default for the t-SNE family, PaCMAP, LocalMAP and PHATE.

Every backend bar "exhaustive" searches in float32, whatever you hand it, and casts the distances back to your dtype. Same recall, less memory traffic. The knobs per backend live in NeighbourParams; only the fields of the backend you picked do anything.

docs.title: Speed¶
docs.text: Every backend at three sizes, one run each.

docs.title: Precision¶
docs.text:
Approximate means approximate. Two numbers against the exhaustive ground truth on 25k points:

  • Recall@k: fraction of the true k neighbours found, in any order.
  • Mean distance ratio: distance to the found neighbour over the distance to the true one at the same rank. 1.0 is perfect, and it tells you how wrong the misses are.

docs.title: Seeding NN-Descent¶
docs.text:
Both NN-Descents start the same way. A forest of random projection trees splits the data into small leaves, every point takes its leaf mates as its first guess at its neighbours, and the descent then refines that graph by checking neighbours of neighbours until few edges change. More trees means a better first guess and fewer descent iterations, at a higher upfront cost.

The two disagree on how many trees to plant. "nndescent" follows scanpy (and umap-learn's compatibility layout): 5 + sqrt(n) / 20, capped at 64. "rinnd" follows PyNNDescent's own default: 2 * log10(n), clamped to [3, 12]. So the ann-search-rs index bets on the forest, with a count that grows with the square root of the data, and rinnd bets on the descent, with a count that barely moves. The gap opens up with the data: about 1.5x at 25k points, twice the trees at 100k, and nearly five times at a million cells.

docs.title: Build once, embed many times¶
docs.text:
On anything large the neighbour search is most of the runtime. Running UMAP with three different min_dist values, plus t-SNE, plus PaCMAP? Build the graph once and pass it in. Each estimator takes knn_indices and knn_distances in fit / fit_transform.

Mind the width. UMAP takes n_neighbors neighbours and cuts a wider graph down (with a warning on stderr). t-SNE wants 3 * perplexity. PaCMAP and LocalMAP want n_near + 50, because the near pairs are the best n_near of a wider search by locally scaled distance. So build the widest one you need.

docs.title: PHATE and diffusion maps
PHATE and diffusion maps¶
docs.text:
Python port of the R vignettes PHATE and Diffusion maps. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

The diffusion family. Both model the data as a random walk over a kNN graph and both were built for continuous structure: trajectories, branch points, manifolds. PHATE lays out potential distances of the diffused walk with MDS, diffusion maps take the eigenvectors of the diffusion operator directly.

docs.title: PHATE¶
docs.text:
PHATE runs in steps. An adaptive-bandwidth kernel over the kNN graph, shaped by decay, gives the affinities. Row-normalise and you have a Markov transition matrix, the diffusion operator. Power it to time t, picked at the knee of the von Neumann entropy unless you pin it. Diffusion denoises: local noise gets smoothed out and the global geometry comes forward. From the diffused transition probabilities PHATE computes a potential distance, the difference of their logs (gamma sets the exact transform), and lays it out with MDS.

Against t-SNE and UMAP:

  • Built for continuous structure. Branching and continuous manifolds survive, where t-SNE and UMAP break them into islands.
  • Distances mean a bit more. The potential distance is a more interpretable metric than either of the others. Still don't over-read it.
  • Fails on genuinely discrete clusters. With no geometry connecting them, PHATE looks for a manifold that isn't there.
  • t matters. Too little diffusion and noise dominates, too much and the fine structure washes out. The entropy knee works well in practice, but look at what you get.

docs.title: Clustered data¶
docs.text: The failure mode first, because it's worth seeing.

docs.title: Pre-computed kNN graphs¶
docs.text: PHATE needs a wider graph than k: neighbours past the k-th join the kernel while their affinity clears the threshold, so the internal search runs 6 * k + 5 wide. Give a pre-computed graph the same width. With the graph fixed, pinning t is cheap to try.

docs.title: Landmarks¶
docs.text:
The full diffusion operator is N x N, and so is the dense potential distance matrix. Landmarks get around that: pick a representative subset, diffuse over it only, and interpolate everything else in. The default is 2048 landmarks (a power of two, for the SIMD in the k-means underneath). landmark_method picks them:

  • "spectral" (default): spectral clustering on the affinity graph. The most representative coverage on complex topology, and the most expensive.
  • "random": uniform. Fast, uneven coverage when the density varies.
  • "density": drawn by dampened node degree. A bit more careful than random, but rare branches can be missed.

500 to 2000 landmarks cover most data up to a few hundred thousand points. Too few and the interpolation misses fine structure, too many and the speed advantage goes. n_landmarks=None runs the full operator, which gets nasty fast on large data.

docs.title: Diffusion maps¶
docs.text:
Same early pipeline as PHATE: a kNN graph, an adaptive Gaussian kernel, and an anisotropic normalisation (alpha) that corrects for uneven sampling. The result is a row-stochastic operator P, a random walk on the manifold. Then the paths split. Instead of diffusing for t steps and computing potential distances, diffusion maps eigendecompose the symmetric form of P. The top non-trivial eigenvectors are the coordinates, scaled by \(\lambda_k^t\), so t ends up as an exponent on the eigenvalues: larger t favours the dominant directions, smaller t keeps more detail.

alpha is the distinctive knob. 0 gives the normalised graph Laplacian, 0.5 the Fokker-Planck operator, 1 (default) the Laplace-Beltrami operator, which recovers the manifold geometry independent of the sampling density.

Against PHATE:

  • More transparent. The coordinates are eigenvectors of a well-defined operator, orthogonal and ordered by importance.
  • Different look. Axis-aligned, symmetric, horseshoes on linear trajectories where PHATE looks organic.
  • Different failure on clusters. With near-disconnected clusters the top eigenvectors approximate cluster indicators.
  • No MDS step, so the embedding is fixed once the operator is.

docs.title: Landmarks¶
docs.text: The same landmark machinery as PHATE: pick a subset, eigendecompose the L x L landmark operator, Nystroem-extend back to everything. Unlike PHATE it is off by default. The full operator stays sparse and goes to a sparse eigensolver, while the landmark operator is dense, so on moderate data the full operator is the faster one. Landmarks are for data where the full operator no longer fits comfortably.

docs.title: Benchmarks¶
docs.text: PHATE against the reference phate package, on all cores, one run each, wall time in seconds. Both run their defaults: k = 5, around 2000 landmarks, entropy-picked t.

docs.title: t-SNE, den-SNE and DREAMS
t-SNE, den-SNE and DREAMS¶
docs.text:
Python port of the R vignettes t-SNE, densMAP and den-SNE and DREAMS. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

The t-SNE family in one place. Plain t-SNE with Barnes-Hut, a quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut and two flavours of FFT-accelerated interpolation. Then the two extensions that fix t-SNE's best known weaknesses: den-SNE keeps relative density, DREAMS keeps the global arrangement.

docs.title: t-SNE¶
docs.text:
t-SNE models pairwise similarities as a Gaussian in the input space and a Student t in the embedding, then minimises the KL divergence between the two. The heavy tails of the t are the trick: dissimilar points can sit far apart without huge gradients, which is what fixes the crowding problem of earlier methods. Compared to UMAP:

  • Better on continuous structure. The loss is symmetric and driven by pairwise probabilities rather than graph connectivity, so it tears continuous manifolds apart less readily. Not immune though, especially at low perplexity.
  • Slower. Naive t-SNE is O(N^2). Barnes-Hut gets it to O(N log N), the FFT versions to O(N) with a bigger constant.
  • Distances in the embedding mean nothing. Cluster sizes and gaps between clusters should not be over-interpreted.

Perplexity is the knob: roughly the effective number of neighbours per point. 5 to 50 is the usual range. Low values chase local structure, high values pull in more of the global picture.

docs.title: Clustered data¶
docs.text: Ten Gaussian clusters in 50 dimensions. PCA first, for a baseline.

docs.title: Swiss roll¶
docs.text: A 2-D sheet rolled up in 3-D, coloured by the position along the roll. We need a higher perplexity here to give the global structure a chance, and with 1000 points an exact search costs nothing.

docs.title: Trajectory¶
docs.text: A branching trajectory in 50 dimensions, coloured by branch. The points are shuffled before plotting so the later branches don't hide the earlier ones.

docs.title: Pre-computed kNN graphs¶
docs.text: Sweeping perplexity or epochs? Compute the graph once. t-SNE wants 3 * perplexity neighbours, so the widest perplexity you plan to try sets k. A graph no wider than perplexity is an error; a wider one is used in full, so slice it (idx[:, :3 * perplexity]) to get the default width.

docs.title: The repulsion approximations¶
docs.text:
The attractive forces only run over the kNN graph and are cheap. The repulsion runs over all pairs and is where the time goes. Four ways to approximate it, picked with approx:

  • "barnes_hut" (default, alias "bh"): a quadtree, O(N log N).
  • "bh_qd" (alias "qd"): the quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut from qdtsne. The tree depth is capped at TsneOptim(max_depth=...) (default 7), and repulsion is computed once per leaf from its centre of mass instead of once per point. A bit less precise, a lot faster. qdtsne recommends depths of 7 to 10.
  • "fft": FIt-SNE. Charges are spread onto an interpolation grid and the repulsion comes out of an FFT convolution. O(N), with a constant that pays off from a few tens of thousands of points.
  • "fft_3k": the three-kernel variant. Put a unit charge on the grid and convolve it with three kernels (q, q^2 dx and q^2 dy), which hands you the normalisation and the forces directly. One forward and three inverse transforms per epoch instead of four and four.

docs.title: den-SNE: keeping density¶
docs.text:
t-SNE carries the same warning as UMAP: cluster sizes in the embedding mean nothing. A blob twice as wide as its neighbour might be ten times tighter in the input. Neither loss has a term that cares how spread out a neighbourhood was to begin with.

den-SNE adds one:

\[-\lambda \cdot \mathrm{Corr}(\log R_o, \log R_e)\]

\(R_o\) is a local radius in the input, a graph-weighted average squared distance to a point's neighbours, and \(R_e\) the matching radius in the embedding. Maximise their correlation and a tight cluster stays tight, a diffuse one stays diffuse. The term only switches on over the last DensParams(frac=...) of the epochs (default 30%), so it corrects a settled layout instead of fighting the initialisation. lambda_ weighs it, and 0 gives you plain t-SNE back.

To see any of this we need to measure local density before and after. A proxy for \(R_o\): the log of the mean squared distance to the 15 nearest neighbours. The cluster generator draws a different spread per cluster, so there is real density variation to keep.

docs.title: DREAMS: keeping the global arrangement¶
docs.text:
t-SNE throws away where the clusters sit relative to each other. DREAMS gets it back with a pull towards a reference layout. Every epoch it scales the usual update by 1 - lambda and adds

\[-\eta \lambda^2 \frac{2}{n} (y - \alpha y_e)\]

\(y_e\) is the centred reference, \(\alpha = \|Y\|_F / \|Y_e\|_F\) rescales it to the current size of the embedding, and \(\eta\) is the automatic openTSNE learning rate. The optimisation starts from the reference too, so init is ignored. lambda_ lives in [0, 1]: 0 is t-SNE started from the reference, 1 returns the reference. The default 0.15 is the paper's. The extra term is O(n) per epoch, so DREAMS costs what t-SNE costs, and every approx works.

Two numbers per embedding. Global: the Spearman correlation between subcluster centroid distances in the input and in the embedding. Local: the fraction of each point's 15 nearest neighbours that survive.

docs.text: A sweep from t-SNE to PCA.

docs.title: Bring your own reference¶
docs.text: PCA is a fine reference when the global structure is linear-ish. When it is not, pass something better via reference in fit: any (n_samples, 2) array. On a branching trajectory PHATE is the obvious pick.

docs.text: Against openTSNE, the fastest t-SNE in Python, on all cores. One run each, wall time in seconds. Mind that the epochs differ: openTSNE runs 250 early exaggeration plus 500 iterations, we run 1000 in total.

docs.title: UMAP, densMAP, PaCMAP, LocalMAP, ForceAtlas2 and NCVis
UMAP, densMAP, PaCMAP, LocalMAP, ForceAtlas2 and NCVis¶
docs.text:
Python port of the R vignettes UMAP, densMAP and den-SNE, PaCMAP and ForceAtlas2. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

The graph layout family. UMAP and its density-preserving sibling densMAP, PaCMAP and its locally adjusted successor LocalMAP, Gephi's ForceAtlas2 and NCVis. All of them start from a kNN graph and pull neighbours together while pushing everything else apart. Where they differ is in what they push and when.

docs.title: UMAP¶
docs.text:
UMAP builds a weighted kNN graph in the input space, where the edge weights say how likely two points are to be connected under a local, adaptive metric (the kNN vignette has the searches). It then minimises the cross-entropy between that graph and its low-dimensional twin, pulling connected points together and pushing unconnected ones apart. That is why UMAP is great at clusters: if two points are unlikely neighbours, the repulsion drives them apart and you get clean separation.

The flip side: UMAP has no incentive to keep relative distances along a continuum. On trajectory-like data the loss treats weakly connected distant points as things to repel, not as part of one structure, and continuous manifolds get torn into spurious clusters. UMAP is a visualisation tool, not a metric space!

The default optimiser is a parallel Adam, the same idea as uwot::umap2(). Each node gathers its gradient and takes its Adam step in one pass, in parallel, so it scales with your cores and the same seed gives the same embedding every time.

docs.title: Clustered data, swiss roll and trajectory¶
docs.text: PCA against UMAP on all three. The trajectory points are shuffled before plotting so the later branches don't hide the earlier ones.

docs.title: Pre-computed kNN graphs¶
docs.text: Sweeping min_dist with the neighbours fixed? Build the graph once and pass it to fit_transform.

docs.title: Optimisers¶
docs.text:
Five of them:

  • "adam_parallel" (default): parallel Adam, reproducible.
  • "adam": the same Adam, single-threaded.
  • "sgd": the classic umap-learn and uwot::umap() SGD with edge sampling. Single-threaded, reproducible.
  • "sgd_parallel": the same SGD lock-free, Hogwild! style. All threads write to the embedding without locks, which is where the speed comes from. The price: with more than one thread it is not reproducible run to run, seed or no seed.
  • "adam_v06": the Adam of umap-learn 0.6, with its own learning rate schedule. Pair it with init="recursive", the umap-learn 0.6 label propagation initialisation, and it takes the short warm-up umap-learn uses for a good start.

Like umap-learn, the SGD optimisers drop to 200 epochs above 10k samples unless you set n_epochs.

docs.title: densMAP¶
docs.text:
Cluster sizes in a UMAP mean nothing. A blob twice as wide as its neighbour might be ten times tighter in the input, because nothing in the loss cares how spread out a neighbourhood was. densMAP adds one term:

\[-\lambda \cdot \mathrm{Corr}(\log R_o, \log R_e)\]

\(R_o\) is a local radius in the input, a graph-weighted average squared distance to a point's neighbours, and \(R_e\) the matching radius in the embedding. Maximise the correlation and a tight cluster stays tight, a diffuse one diffuse. Same graph, same repulsion, same optimisers otherwise. The knobs:

  • lambda_: weight of the density term, 2.0 by default. 0 gives plain UMAP back.
  • DensParams(frac=...): fraction of the epochs, at the end, over which the term runs. 0.3 by default; switching it on from epoch zero fights the initialisation. Over the last 30% only, so you pay maybe a third more wall time.
  • DensParams(var_shift=...): a shift on the variance of the embedding log-radii that keeps the correlation sane when the radii collapse.

The umap-learn 0.6 Adam has no density term, so densMAP refuses "adam_v06".

To see any of this we need local density before and after. A proxy for \(R_o\): the log of the mean squared distance to the 15 nearest neighbours.

docs.title: Density along a manifold¶
docs.text: Clusters are the easy case. The biased swiss roll samples non-uniformly along the roll, so the density gradient is continuous rather than blocky.

docs.title: Tuning lambda¶
docs.text: The usual framing is that lambda_ trades cluster separation for density fidelity. Let's check on 2000 points. Separation here is the mean distance between cluster centroids over the mean distance of a point to its own centroid.

docs.title: PaCMAP¶
docs.text:
PaCMAP builds its embedding from three kinds of pair. Near pairs keep local neighbourhoods. Mid-near pairs, the second closest of six random points, are a medium-range pull that anchors the global structure. Further pairs, random distant points minus the near pairs, push.

The trick is the phased schedule. In phase one the mid-near weight decays from 1000 to 3, which pulls points into a globally coherent arrangement before any local structure is resolved. In phase two it holds at 3 while the near weight rises, so local structure emerges without wrecking the layout. Phase three runs on near and further pairs only. UMAP optimises one objective from the start; PaCMAP settles the global picture first.

Three things to know:

  • PCA initialisation. Random init throws away most of the global structure, hence init="pca" by default.
  • n_near is less touchy than UMAP's n_neighbors. The paper's 10 works across a wide range of data. The search runs n_near + 50 wide and the near pairs are the best of those by locally scaled distance, so a pre-computed graph should be n_near + 50 wide too.
  • Mid-near pairs don't come from the graph. They are sampled.

docs.title: LocalMAP¶
docs.text:
LocalMAP is PaCMAP with a different phase three. Further pairs that already sit more than max_distance apart in the embedding get resampled (they have done their job), and the near-pair forces are scaled by their embedding distance. The upshot: clusters PaCMAP leaves touching get pulled apart, and the global arrangement from the first two phases stays. Same arguments as PaCMAP, plus max_distance (default 10).

The hierarchical data is where the difference between UMAP and the PaCMAP family shows. 16 subclusters in 4 supergroups, in 50 dimensions.

docs.title: Pre-computed kNN and the phase schedule¶
docs.text: With the graph fixed you can play with the schedule. Here phase one runs to epoch 300 instead of 100, so the mid-near pairs dominate for much longer.

docs.title: ForceAtlas2¶
docs.text:
Gephi's force-directed layout, known in single cell from scanpy's draw_graph and PAGA-initialised layouts. ForceAtlas2 treats the graph as a physical system. Every node repels every other with a force of 1/d, scaled by the node masses (1 + degree, so hubs push harder). Every edge pulls its ends together, linearly with distance or logarithmically with lin_log=True. Gravity pulls everything to the origin so disconnected components don't drift off. Step sizes follow Gephi's adaptive speed, and the all-pairs repulsion runs on a Barnes-Hut tree.

How is that different from UMAP? UMAP samples edges and negatives and minimises a loss. ForceAtlas2 visits every edge every epoch and has no loss, just forces. No min_dist or spread either: the scale of the layout falls out of scaling_ratio (repulsion) against the edge weights (attraction). It runs on the same fuzzy union graph UMAP builds, as scanpy does, and needs it symmetric, so UmapGraph(mix_weight=...) has to stay at 1.

docs.title: NCVis¶
docs.text:
NCVis (Artemenkov & Panov, 2020) swaps UMAP's cross-entropy for noise-contrastive estimation. The graph is the plain kNN graph, made undirected, with no weights at all. Each edge pulls its two points together and draws uniform negatives that push apart, each weighted by how likely the pair is data rather than noise. The normalisation constant that makes that a proper probability is learned on the side, as one more parameter. The negatives ramp up with the cube of progress, so the early epochs mostly attract and the late ones do most of the pushing.

The defaults are Sean Pedersen's NCVis+, whose kernel this is a port of: a PCA start scaled as a whole to std 10 on its first axis, min_dist 0.001, learning rate 2, 50 epochs and on average 10 negatives per edge. The PCA start is the one that matters for global structure, and like for PaCMAP it is the default for that reason. The optimiser is hogwild, so a fixed seed reproduces only on one thread (mf.set_num_threads(1)).

The original NCVis start is there too, as init="ncvis": uniform noise, then 20 passes that replace every point by the sum of its neighbours and standardise each axis. A cheap graph smoothing, no eigensolver in sight. It gets the same init_scale as the other starts.

Back to the hierarchical data, against UMAP and PaCMAP.

docs.title: Benchmarks¶
docs.text:
Against umap-learn 0.6 and the reference PaCMAP package (which also ships LocalMAP), on all cores. One run each, wall time in seconds, neighbour search included. Both references compile with numba on first use, so they get a warm-up call on a small dataset before the clock starts.

Like for like where it exists: umap-learn's default 0.6 path (recursive init and Adam) against our "adam_v06" with init="recursive", and its legacy SGD layout against our "sgd_parallel", which is equally non-reproducible.
